text: (Places picture of dining room)
speaker: C1

text: Lunch with Aunt Agatha.
speaker: C1

text: Lord Henry passed up the low arcade into Burlington Street and turned his steps in the direction of Berkeley Square.
speaker: LORD H

text: As he walked, he contemplated the story of Dorian Gray's parentage.
speaker: C2

text: Crudely as it had been told to him, it had yet stirred him by its suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance.
speaker: C3

text: It posed the lad, made him more perfect, as it were. Talking to him was like playing upon an exquisite violin.
speaker: C4

text: There was something terribly enthralling in the exercise of influence.
speaker: LORD H

text: Yes; he would try to be to Dorian Gray what, without knowing it, the lad was to the painter who had fashioned the wonderful portrait.
speaker: C1

text: He would seek to dominate him — had already, indeed, half done so. He would make that wonderful spirit his own.
speaker: C2

text: Suddenly he stopped.
speaker: All

text: and glanced up at the houses.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: He found that he had passed his aunt’s by some distance.
speaker: C3

text: and, smiling to himself, turned back.
speaker: LORD H

text: When he entered the somewhat sombre hall, the butler told him that they had gone in to lunch. He gave him his hat and stick and passed into the dining-room.
speaker: C4

text: Late as usual, Harry.
speaker: Lady A

text: He invented an excuse and took the vacant seat next to her and looked around the table.
speaker: C1

text: Dorian bowed shyly to him from the end of the table, a flush of pleasure stealing into his cheek.
speaker: C2

text: Here was the Duchess of Harley, much liked by all who knew her.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: Lord H was pleased to see Mr Erskine of Treadley, a gentleman of considerable charm and culture.
speaker: MR E

text: Here was Sir Thomas Burdon who had an opinion on everything
speaker: SIR T

text: and had been boring his listeners throughout the luncheon. The Duchess was relieved to see Lord Henry.
speaker: C2

text: We are talking about poor Dartmoor, Lord Henry. Do you think he will really marry this fascinating young person?
speaker: DUCHESS

text: I believe she has made up her mind to propose to him, Duchess
speaker: LORD H

text: How dreadful! Really, someone should interfere.
speaker: Lady A

text: I am told, on excellent authority, that her father keeps an American dry-goods store
speaker: SIR T

text: Dry-goods! What are American dry-goods.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: American novels
speaker: LORD H

text: Don't mind him, my dear, he never means anything that he says.
speaker: Lady A

text: When America was discovered……
speaker: SIR T

text: I wish to goodness it never had been discovered at all! Really, our girls have no chance nowadays. It is most unfair.
speaker: Lady A

text: Perhaps, after all, America never has been discovered, I myself would say that it had merely been detected.
speaker: MR E

text: Oh! but I have seen specimens of the inhabitants and I must confess that most of them are extremely pretty. And they dress well, too. They get all their dresses in Paris. I wish I could afford to do the same.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: They say that when good Americans die they go to Paris
speaker: SIR T

text: Really! And where do bad Americans go to when they die?
speaker: DUCHESS

text: They go to America.
speaker: LORD H

text: I am afraid that your nephew is prejudiced against that great country. I have travelled all over. I assure you that it is an education to visit it.
speaker: SIR T

text: But must we really see Chicago in order to be educated? I don't feel up to the journey.
speaker: MR E

text: Mr. Erskine has the world on his shelves. We practical men like to see things, not to read about them. The Americans are an extremely interesting people. They are absolutely reasonable.
speaker: SIR T

text: How dreadful! I can stand brute force, but brute reason is quite unbearable. There is something unfair about its use. It is hitting below the intellect.
speaker: LORD H

text: I do not understand you
speaker: SIR T

text: I do.
speaker: MR E

text: Dear me! how you men argue! I am sure I never can make out what you are talking about. And Harry, I am quite vexed with you. Why do you try to persuade our nice Mr. Dorian Gray to give up the East End? I assure you he would be quite invaluable. They would love his playing.
speaker: Lady A

text: I want him to play to me.
speaker: LORD H

text: But they are so unhappy in Whitechapel.
speaker: Lady A

text: I can sympathise with everything except suffering. Suffering is too ugly, too horrible, too distressing. The less said about life’s sores, the better.
speaker: LORD H

text: Still, the East End is a very important problem.
speaker: SIR T

text: Quite so. It is the problem of slavery, and we try to solve it by amusing the slaves.
speaker: LORD H

text: What change do you propose, then?
speaker: SIR T

text: I don't desire to change anything in England except the weather. As the nineteenth century has gone bankrupt through an over-expenditure of sympathy, I would suggest that we should appeal to science to put us straight.
speaker: LORD H

text: But we have such grave responsibilities,
speaker: Lady A

text: Humanity takes itself too seriously. It is the world's original sin. If the caveman had known how to laugh, history would have been different.
speaker: LORD H

text: You are really very comforting, I have always felt rather guilty when I came to see your dear aunt, for I take no interest at all in the East End. For the future I shall be able to look her in the face without a blush.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: A blush is very becoming, Duchess.
speaker: LORD H

text: Only when one is young. When an old woman like myself blushes, it is a very bad sign. Ah! Lord Henry, I wish you would tell me how to become young again.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: Can you remember any great error that you committed in your early days?
speaker: LORD H

text: A great many, I fear.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: Then commit them over again. To get back one's youth, one has merely to repeat one's follies.
speaker: LORD H

text: A delightful theory! I must put it into practice.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: A dangerous theory!
speaker: SIR T

text: Your carriage is waiting your Grace
speaker: Butler

text: How annoying! I must go. I have to call for my husband at the club, If I am late he is sure to be furious, and I couldn’t have a scene in this bonnet. It is far too fragile. A harsh word would ruin it. No, I must go, dear Agatha. Good-bye, Lord Henry, you are quite delightful and dreadfully demoralising. You must come and dine with us some night. Tuesday? Are you disengaged Tuesday?
speaker: DUCHESS

text: For you I would throw over anybody.
speaker: LORD H

text: Ah! that is very nice, and very wrong of you, so mind you come.
speaker: DUCHESS

text: And now I must bid good-bye to your excellent Aunt. I am due at the Athenaeum. It is the hour when we sleep there.
speaker: MR E

text: All of you, Mr. Erskine?
speaker: LORD H

text: Forty of us, in forty arm-chairs. We are practising for an English Academy of Letters.
speaker: MR E

text: I am going to the park.
speaker: LORD H

text: Let me come with you.
speaker: Dorian

text: But I thought you had promised Basil Hallward you would go and see him.
speaker: LORD H

text: I would sooner come with you. Yes, I feel I must come with you. Do let me. And you will promise to talk to me all the time? No one talks so wonderfully as you do.
speaker: Dorian

text: Ah! I have talked quite enough for to-day. All I want now is to look at life. You may come and look at it with me, if you care to.
speaker: LORD H
